title: Evolve a single-machine key-value store
description: Build around an existing high-performance store to provide scalable, durable, highly available put/get/delete operations without rewriting the local storage engine.
focus: sharding, metadata and routing, replicated writes, safe failover, online data movement, and strong-consistency follow-ups.

children.value: Turn a single-machine KV store into always-on infrastructure.
Preserve the existing storage engine. Add the placement, routing, replication, recovery, and operational machinery needed to serve a billion keys across hundreds of machines.
Based on your supplied prompt and evaluation notes, using the same progressive delivery style as the previous guide. Proposed policies and numerical scenarios are distinguished from givens.
Existing store → multiple shards → cached routing and metadata → replicas → safe acknowledgments and failover → online movement → optional strong reads.
The key interview skill is explaining
what owns a key, what makes a write durable, and why those answers remain correct while machines fail or data moves
. Naming consistent hashing and quorums is only the beginning.
Do not design a new storage engine

A mature single-machine store already has excellent local performance, but one node limits availability, durability, and capacity. We must build a distributed service around it while preserving a simple

Treat local key lookup, value storage, deletion, and the engine's internal implementation as existing capabilities. Do not spend the interview designing an LSM tree, B-tree, Bloom filter, or disk compaction algorithm.
Partition ownership, replica placement, routing, metadata, write ordering, durable replication, failover, rebalancing, recovery, and safe operation during topology changes.

The prompt calls this the “control plane.” More precisely, metadata and placement are control-plane responsibilities; request routing and replication also execute on the serving path. The important boundary is that
the local persistence engine remains unchanged

single-key create/overwrite, lookup, and delete. No client-visible transactions, compare-and-swap, scans, or bulk APIs. Internal coordination may still use consensus or atomic metadata updates; excluding client CAS does not prohibit safe internal coordination.

“I will keep the existing engine as a black box. First I will distribute keys and route requests so all three operations work across machines. Then I will add replication and explain write acknowledgment, failover, and movement. I will use eventual reads for the base workload and cover strong single-key reads as a follow-up.”
Separate supplied limits from the choices still open
P99 reads: 1 ms. Throughput: 10K QPS per machine.
Use as an initial bound, but clarify the benchmark's value sizes, read/write mix, and concurrency. Do not assume every maximum occurs together.
Replication and operating headroom multiply the physical footprint. Multiple engine instances on one host share this machine-level budget.
Keep wrapper metadata out of the opaque application value, or explicitly account for any representation change. A 1 GB value is a separate follow-up.
Up to 1M QPS; more than 90% reads. Of writes, about 90% overwrite existing data and 10% create new data.
Read replicas help; overwrites still generate replication/log traffic. New-key growth cannot continue forever without deletions or admission control.
Up to 1 billion pairs; up to 1 PB logical data.
Plan storage and cardinality independently; central metadata must not contain a per-key routing row for every key.
P90 reads in tens of milliseconds; P90 writes in hundreds of milliseconds.
Leaves room for routing and regional replication, but requires bounded queues and attention to payload/network cost.
At least 99.99% availability; durability as high as possible.
Define failure domains, the acknowledgment boundary, recovery objectives, backups, and the behavior when a quorum cannot be reached.
Eventual consistency is acceptable; strong consistency is a follow-up.
Default reads can use applied replica state. Strong reads require an additional protocol, not simply a “strong” flag on the same local read.
A change-data stream can be assumed if requested.
Useful for asynchronous replication or migration, but its ordering, resume point, retention, and durability still need a contract.
These are questions to ask the interviewer; the working choices below are not additional facts in the prompt.
Which failures must an acknowledged write survive?
“As durable as possible” is not a finite engineering contract.
Three replicas in distinct zones; no loss of quorum-committed writes after one replica/zone failure. Independent backups address larger disasters and logical mistakes.
Must both sides of a network partition keep accepting writes?
Determines whether coordinated writes are acceptable or conflicting versions must be reconciled.
Majority-side writes continue; minority-side writes fail or time out. Explain a Dynamo-style alternative if partition-time write availability is mandatory.
What are request-weighted average sizes, skew, and burst duration?
1M tiny requests and 1M near-1MB requests have radically different network costs.
Show both a small-value case and a ceiling-size stress case rather than invent an average.
What local durability, atomicity, and operational export facilities exist?
Recovery and migration need more than an undocumented successful return from
Assume atomic local single-key operations and a supported durable checkpoint/backup mechanism. Internal iteration/export is needed for filtering existing data during shard splits.
Can we route every mutation through the new layer?
Untracked legacy writes bypass replication and ordering.
Yes, through a compatible endpoint/proxy rollout. Fence direct engine access before claiming the new guarantees.
a client can create or overwrite one key and receive a precisely defined write result.
a client can retrieve one value or a genuine not-found result under the chosen consistency mode.
a client can remove one key; retries, failover, and movement must not accidentally resurrect it.
If the old store truly exposes only opaque

, with no key enumeration, usable backup, change stream, or access to a supported checkpoint, you cannot discover and migrate arbitrary existing keys by guessing their names. Clarify that operational capability. Client-facing “no scans” does not normally forbid internal backup/export, but the distinction must be explicit.

one committed mutation order per shard; one authoritative ownership configuration; no application of uncommitted log entries; no successful durability acknowledgment before the stated replication boundary; no false not-found on backend failure; and no independently writable old and new owners during a move.
For AE, make the reasoning visible
Use the same progression as your reference example:
working behavior → visible limitation → alternatives → justified change → revised flow
. Follow the interviewer notes by building sharding/routing before going deep into replication.
Your Senior IC3 AE target means meeting all six evaluation axes and exceeding at least two, including
. This answer concentrates its strongest signals in
Illustrative 45-minute schedule. The document is a study reference, not a script to read in full.
Confirm the engine boundary, public operations, failure scope, consistency, and workload assumptions.
Storage and QPS floors, replication factor, payload sensitivity, and headroom.
Key/value, shard, replica, map, mutation, and simple put/get/delete contracts.
Draw routing, placement metadata, and the unchanged engines. Trace all three operations.
Add replica groups, define acknowledgment/apply points, and trace retry/failover.
Online movement plus strong-read/quorum reasoning; reserve a short branch for hot keys or recovery bandwidth.
Map the design back to SLOs; state partition, cost, and stale-read trade-offs.
Do not spend five minutes debating REST versus gRPC.
The interface is deliberately simple. Spend that time on where a request goes, who may acknowledge it, and what happens when ownership changes.

“I will first get the distributed key lookup and write paths working, leaving replication as a visible gap. Then I will close that gap and use the remaining time on the two subtle cases: moving a shard while writes continue and avoiding stale or unsafe results during failover.”
Hundreds of machines is a floor, not a complete capacity plan
Use decimal KB/MB/TB/PB for this estimate. Use a rounded
as a write-heavy boundary case for the supplied read-heavy workload. Assume replication factor
; 70% target disk occupancy is an illustrative operating policy, not a given.
Full-disk storage floor = 3 PB / 10 TB = 300 machines
At 70% disk occupancy = ceil(3 PB / 7 TB) = 429 machines

storage dominates this simple floor. It does not justify declaring “429 machines is enough.” Logs, backups, indexes, replica repair, request skew, network, CPU, and failure-time traffic still need budget. An explicit cap of 100 machines would not fit 1 PB with three full copies on 10 TB nodes.
The maximums expose useful follow-up questions
At both storage/cardinality ceilings, the average stored pair is near the maximum value size. Do not simultaneously model that dataset as all 1KB values.
A small-value traffic scenario, excluding keys and protocol overhead.
A ceiling-size stress case: roughly 7.2 Tb/s before overhead. Proxies and NICs must scale too.
Two follower copies add about 200 GB/s of replication payload, plus client/proxy hops and log/apply I/O.
10% new keys, if writes are PUTs
Without offsetting deletes, a billion-key budget fills from empty in about 27.78 hours at that sustained rate.
10 TB repair at 100 MB/s usable copy rate
An illustrative bandwidth calculation: failure exposure depends on recovery time, not just replica count.

Stored average size does not determine request-weighted average size: small hot values might dominate requests while large cold values dominate disk. Ask about both. The ceilings can be valid peak limits without being a sustainable simultaneous steady state.
Overwrites are not free: log retention can dominate
Even if a put replaces an existing value, the replication log carries the new bytes. At the
above, a full-payload log replicated three ways has the following budget, in addition to the materialized dataset:

These figures exclude other overhead and assume the entire peak is sustained for the retention period. They explain why “just retain a day of Kafka” is not a capacity-free answer. Checkpoint state, compact/truncate safely, and resnapshot lagging replicas rather than retain every overwrite indefinitely.

of full-outage time. This is only a time-equivalent illustration: define the actual request-based SLI, read/write treatment, timeouts, and partial failures. Three replicas do not mathematically guarantee four nines.
Small public API; explicit distributed semantics
Opaque application bytes. Key/value limits and authorization belong at the distributed boundary.
Stable shard ID and hash range; unit of replication, recovery, placement, and most rebalancing.
Node identity, zone/rack, health, capacity, replica role, and applied log position. A physical node hosts many shard replicas.
Hash range → shard/group ID → replica endpoints, leader hint, and configuration epoch.
Request ID, operation, original key/value, and an ordered shard-log position.
Shard ID, configuration, engine checkpoint, included log index, and wrapper recovery/deduplication state.

put(key: bytes, value: bytes) -> write_receipt
get(key: bytes)              -> value | NOT_FOUND
delete(key: bytes)           -> write_receipt

SDK / request metadata, without adding new public operations:
    request_id        stable across retries of a mutation
    deadline          bounded end-to-end retry budget
    route_epoch       cached configuration version

Write receipt:
    shard_id
    committed_index
    durability_status

Optional follow-up:
    get(key, consistency = EVENTUAL | LINEARIZABLE)
    get(key, minimum_observed_position = receipt)
The base API stays simple; request IDs and routing metadata can live in SDK context or headers. A mutation timeout is
: it may have committed. Retrying the same request ID can recover the result. A transport error must not become

success means the operation is committed in the shard's replicated log. Materialization can lag. A default eventual read may therefore return an older value or an old not-found result; an optional receipt-based barrier or linearizable read addresses that use case.

Log indices and configuration epochs are protocol state, not wall-clock timestamps. Concurrent puts are serialized by the shard's committed order, not by whichever machine reports the largest wall-clock time. No cross-key atomicity is promised.

Store original keys and values unchanged in the local engine in the base design. Keep log, configuration, applied-index, and deduplication metadata in the wrapper's own durable state. Do not silently wrap a maximum 1MB application value in extra metadata and then claim it still fits the same engine limit. Transport/log records must allow the payload plus their own headers.
Make all three operations work across machines first
1. Start with the component we already have

props.aria-label: A client invokes the existing local key-value store

children.value: a healthy machine can store, retrieve, overwrite, and delete a key efficiently.
one node caps capacity/QPS; node downtime interrupts service; disk loss can destroy the only copy. Do not redesign local storage to address these distributed problems.
2. Partition keys and add a routing layer

props.aria-label: Applications use a router to choose a storage machine, each running the existing engine

children.value: Hash a key to an owner and forward its operation. Different keys can now live on different machines. A put changes only that owner's local store; a get and a delete use the exact same ownership function.

demonstrates basic distribution, but changing the node count remaps most keys. Under uniform hashing, changing a simple modulo layout from four nodes to five remaps roughly 80% of keys. Old data does not relocate itself when the formula changes.
3. Separate key placement from physical machines

props.aria-label: The router maps a key to a logical shard and uses cached shard metadata to reach the current owner

children.value: Introduce many logical hash ranges and a placement directory. A separate management service assigns ranges to nodes and publishes versioned changes. Routers cache the map; a request does not synchronously ask the manager where every key lives.
put, get, and delete across a growing fleet. Adding a node can move selected logical shards rather than rehash the entire dataset. New shard replicas will later use this same directory.
each shard has one copy; metadata needs high availability; moving live data needs a protocol; clients can have stale routes. These are explicit next steps, not hidden assumptions.

“We now have a complete sharded healthy-path design without changing the engine. I will harden the directory and placement mechanics, then replace each single owner with a replica group and define exactly when writes may succeed.”
Explain the indirection, not just the hash function

a directory of stable virtual hash ranges, with each range mapped to a shard replica group. This gives predictable migration units and lets management account for bytes, read/write load, and failure domains.

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes is a common way to represent such ownership. A fixed initial set of fine-grained hash buckets plus a mutable placement directory is another. The essential property is
two-stage routing: key → logical shard → current placement
, not modulo by the changing physical node count.
Very simple, acceptable as a short baseline.
Membership changes remap a large fraction of keys. Data movement and stale routes remain unresolved.
Many ranges per physical node improve statistical balance and allow incremental reassignment.
A ring alone does not detect hot keys, transfer bytes, preserve write ownership, or ensure zone-aware replica placement.
Explicit migration units, controlled rebalancing, and placement based on multiple resource dimensions.
Requires a reliable metadata service and safe map/configuration transitions.
Highest-scoring node/group wins; limited remapping on membership changes; weights can represent capacity.
Naively scoring every physical node per key is costly at larger fleets. Replica diversity and live movement still require explicit policy.
Useful if ordered scans become important later.
Sequential or skewed keys can create hot ranges. No scan requirement currently earns that complication.

h = hash(original_key)
shard = lookup_hash_range(h)
placement = shard_map[shard]

shard_map[S17] = {
    hash_range: [a, b),
    replicas: [node-12 / zone-A, node-47 / zone-B, node-83 / zone-C],
    leader_hint: node-12,
    configuration_epoch: 42,
    state: SERVING
}
Start with a suitably large number of logical ranges, such as
in a capacity scenario. At 1 PB this averages
. Three copies imply 12,288 shard replicas spread across the fleet. This is an illustrative trade-off between movement size and per-shard metadata, log, heartbeat, and engine-instance overhead.
For the original single-machine deployment, begin with its existing range and split/export it incrementally. A 4,096-shard target is not an assumption that all existing keys are already partitioned.
Independent write order, failover, and repair per shard; replica placement can enforce distinct failure domains.
Manage many groups efficiently, often multiplexing their work within storage-node processes.
Replicate to successors on a ring
Natural preference lists and a compact placement rule.
Successor selection must skip the same physical host/failure domain; membership changes alter both ownership and replica sets.
Balance bytes, read QPS, write QPS, network, and repair load instead of only token counts.
More control-plane complexity and potential oscillation; use hysteresis, rate limits, and explicit placement constraints.

A replica group is not necessarily a dedicated three-machine cluster. Each physical machine hosts replicas from many groups, while no two copies of the same shard share the same required failure domain.
The manager must not become a per-request bottleneck
No proxy hop; less network duplication and proxy infrastructure; routing work naturally scales with clients.
Many languages and versions must implement refresh, redirects, retries, auth, and topology changes correctly.
Centralize compatible client behavior, map refresh, connection pooling, quotas, and retry policy without changing every application.
An extra hop and substantial proxy/network capacity at large payloads. Proxies must scale horizontally and avoid unbounded buffering.

I would start with server-side routing because the existing store has many applications and compatibility matters. Later, well-supported clients can use direct routing with the same storage-side protocol.
A proxy simplifies operations; it does not create consistency.
Both designs need storage-side ownership enforcement.
Maintain shard ranges, replica membership, placement/configuration epochs, node identities and failure domains, migration state, and capacity/health observations. Store
routing records rather than a billion per-key locations.

Use a small strongly consistent metadata cluster, for example three controllers across three zones, with one active placement coordinator. Its availability is independent of one coordinator process. Routers receive snapshots and versioned updates, recovering with a fresh snapshot if an incremental watch falls behind its retained history.
What if the cached route is wrong?
The proxy sends the shard ID and known configuration epoch with the request.
A contacted replica validates whether it can serve the requested operation under its current group state. A stale leader hint is a hint, not authority.
It redirects the proxy to a known current leader/placement or returns an explicit stale-configuration response. The proxy refreshes and retries within the original deadline.
Storage-layer replication and ownership fencing prevent old owners from committing unauthorized writes. Changing a router cache is not sufficient fencing.

the map's configuration epoch identifies placement; a consensus term identifies an election generation; a log index identifies an ordered mutation. They are related protocol state, not interchangeable version numbers.

If metadata is temporarily unavailable, known healthy groups can still serve through cached endpoints and their own replication protocol. New placement, unknown-route requests, and reconfiguration may pause. If all cached endpoints are unreachable, the cache cannot conjure a route.
Add copies, then make their guarantees precise
4. Add an active node and asynchronous followers

props.aria-label: The active storage node writes locally and sends its changes asynchronously to read replicas

children.value: This uses the optional engine change stream. Followers improve read capacity and provide recovery copies. The active serializes mutations, and followers apply them in source order.

if the client is acknowledged after only the active's local write, the active can fail permanently before any follower receives that write. A follower promotion can then lose an acknowledged value. An election by itself does not recreate the missing data.
5. Acknowledge an ordered, replicated commit instead

props.aria-label: The shard leader commits a mutation to a durable quorum log before replicas apply it to the existing engines

children.value: use an established per-shard replicated-log/consensus implementation, such as Raft, in the wrapper. A leader proposes each mutation; replicas durably persist log records; the protocol determines commitment; only committed entries are applied to the engines.

With three voters, a durable majority is two. The third can catch up later. Client success means the committed operation can survive one replica failure, not that every replica has already materialized it.

Default gets can still read applied follower state and remain eventual. This deliberately combines coordinated, durable writes with read scaling; the system does not claim strong reads until we add a read protocol.
The price of the chosen durability boundary

Without a reachable majority, this design cannot acknowledge new writes. That is a conscious partition-time availability trade-off. If the interviewer requires both partitions to remain writable, discuss leaderless replication and conflict resolution rather than claiming Raft provides that behavior.
A simple decoupled write path; replay and independent materialization; acceptable eventual reads.

The queue itself needs durability and ordering. Every replica must receive each relevant mutation, not compete in one work-queue consumer group where only one gets it. Bound lag, retention, and bootstrap recovery.
Simple single-authority reads and writes; CDC can populate the standby.
Read throughput remains limited to the active. Safe failover and acknowledgment durability are not automatic with asynchronous CDC.
Good fit for the read-heavy workload; eventual follower reads can spread load.
Replication lag, missing acknowledged writes under async failover, and stale leader fencing still require policy.
Ordered durable writes, controlled failover, eventual scalable reads, and a path to linearizable reads.
Majority availability, log/checkpoint machinery, safe membership changes, and per-shard coordination overhead.
Can favor write availability during partitions, using versions and later reconciliation.
Concurrent versions, read repair, hinted handoff, anti-entropy, delete/tombstone retention, and application-compatible conflict semantics.

Choosing Raft means using a tested implementation, not designing its elections from scratch. Still explain why commitment, log ordering, and election rules preserve acknowledged data. “Raft handles it” without that explanation earns little depth signal.
Trace every operation to a state change and a response
The proxy authenticates the caller, validates sizes/quotas, hashes the key, and routes to the shard leader with a stable request ID.
The leader checks its authority and retry state, appends
to its replicated log, and sends it to followers.
Followers durably record entries. The consensus protocol commits an eligible prefix after the required majority acknowledgment; a network send or RAM-only acknowledgment is insufficient.

The client receives a receipt identifying the committed operation. An engine-applied acknowledgment could be chosen instead if immediate leader visibility is part of the contract, at additional latency.

Each replica applies committed mutations in order to its unchanged engine, checking duplicate IDs as part of that ordered application. A proposal-side cache is only an optimization: even if a retry is appended twice, the second entry must not mutate the value again. Applied positions and deduplication state are recovered consistently with that order.

A put replaces the previous value according to committed shard order. Distinct concurrent puts are not silently treated as duplicate requests. No user-level CAS or multi-key transaction is introduced.
The proxy locates the shard and chooses an eligible replica based on health/load and the requested consistency mode.
For the default eventual mode, the replica reads its already-applied engine state. Lag indicators can guide routing, but an eventual contract is not automatically a hard staleness bound.
Return the value or a real not-found result from that state. Backend timeout, overload, or an unknown shard is an error, not an empty value.
For read-your-writes, wait for a suitable replica to apply at least the receipt's position or use the leader/strong-read path. Tokens must remain meaningful across configuration changes and splits.
A delete is a replicated mutation,
, ordered and committed like a put. Apply it through the existing engine's delete operation. Repeating deletion of an absent key can be successful, but a retried
delete must not erase a later put as though it were a new request.

A default eventual read can briefly return a pre-delete value from a lagging follower; a strong read after a completed delete must not. During recovery/movement, replay the delete in order. Copying only currently present values and ignoring deletes can resurrect removed keys.
Why request deduplication matters even for put/delete

1. Request A: put(k, "old") commits, but its response is lost.
2. Request B: put(k, "new") commits successfully.
3. Client retries request A with its original request_id.

Correct: return A's existing result; do not overwrite "new".
Incorrect: treat the retry as a fresh put just because put is
           superficially idempotent when no other write intervenes.

Recover retry state from the replicated log/checkpoint. A retry whose original operation is committed but not yet reflected in an applied result may need to wait or consult the committed log; do not infer “new request” from a lagging result cache. Return the canonical operation's receipt. Bound retry-state storage and document the supported retry horizon; indefinite deduplication of arbitrary old IDs is not free. Beyond that horizon, callers must reconcile rather than assume an old retry is harmless.
Received ≠ locally persisted ≠ quorum committed ≠ applied on a replica ≠ visible under a particular read mode.
State which boundary the client response promises.
Recover the wrapper without changing the local engine

A replicated log is useful only if its committed order is safely reflected in the existing engine. The wrapper owns that bridge. It does not require the public engine API to support a transaction across application keys.
Apply committed commands in a recoverable order
Serialize application of committed mutations within each shard replica. Do not expose speculative, uncommitted writes through the engine.
Apply put/delete to the engine and obtain the engine's documented durability boundary, or retain sufficient log to rebuild from a known durable checkpoint.

Advance a durable applied checkpoint only when all state it represents, including required wrapper retry state, is safely recoverable. Never persist “applied through 80” while the durable engine may contain only 75.
On restart, restore a consistent checkpoint and replay the committed suffix. Keep the recovering replica ineligible to serve until its engine and wrapper state reach a consistent advertised point.

A crash after the engine applies a put but before its checkpoint advances can cause replay. A serialized sequence of deterministic put/delete operations can be replayed safely to the recovered committed position. Do not serve the intermediate state while replay temporarily revisits an older put before a later overwrite/delete.

If the engine's successful return is not durable and it provides no usable flush/checkpoint boundary, the wrapper cannot safely truncate its log based on that return. Keep the necessary replay history or clarify the required operational capability rather than assuming durability.

A shard snapshot includes a consistent engine checkpoint plus the matching included log position, configuration, and required wrapper metadata/deduplication state. Publish its manifest atomically only after its components are durable. Install snapshots into a fresh or safely replaced engine image, not by unioning their keys with stale target contents.

Truncate a log prefix only when recovery can start from a durable checkpoint that includes it. A follower beyond the retained suffix needs a new snapshot. It must not force unlimited log retention or rejoin by guessing which operations it missed.

One workable layout uses a separate existing-engine instance/data directory for each shard replica, with wrapper state beside it. That makes whole-shard checkpoint/copy/delete operations tractable without prefixing 1KB user keys or inflating 1MB user values. Many replicas share each physical node's aggregate QPS, RAM, and 10TB budget.

If many engine instances are too expensive, use a supported shard export/checkpoint facility in a shared engine. Do not assume the ability to split/filter opaque internal files without an engine-supported interface.

Route and capture all writes through the new layer, take a supported consistent snapshot with a matching change/log position, restore target replicas, and replay changes after that position. For a stream that cannot be atomically paired with a snapshot, use a documented brief write barrier or another supported backup protocol. Arbitrarily copying live files can produce an inconsistent base.
Only cut over applications once the intended write authority and required replicas are ready. A new log contains future mutations; it cannot reconstruct untouched keys that predate the log.
What happens when a component fails?
Use another stateless proxy; retry within the deadline with the same mutation ID.
A lost response does not prove the mutation failed. Load-balancing infrastructure also needs redundant instances.
Remaining majority can commit. Recover the follower from its persisted log/checkpoint and replay the missing suffix.
Do not count it as caught up just because its process responds to a health check.
The shard's consensus protocol elects an eligible leader; proxies follow the new leader hint.
Election rules must preserve committed history. “Promote the first healthy replica” can lose acknowledged writes.
The client retries; the new/current leader resolves the stable request ID against recoverable retry state.
Do not execute the old mutation again after intervening writes.
The majority component can elect/retain leadership and commit; an isolated former leader cannot commit new mutations.
Minority writes fail/time out. Eventual reads may be stale under the chosen policy; strong reads need current authority.
Create replacement replicas from consistent snapshots plus log catch-up, then change membership safely.
Durability exposure lasts until replication is restored. Copy time, survivor load, and failure-domain diversity matter.
One replica per shard was in that zone; the other two can form a majority if healthy and connected.
Provision the surviving fleet for redirected traffic. Three copies placed in only two remaining zones do not restore the original three-zone protection.
Serve known reachable groups with cached maps and existing group membership; pause placement changes and unknown-route work.
A cache is not a substitute for a new authoritative configuration or unreachable endpoints.
Disk full or apply lag grows
Use admission control, reserved headroom, bounded queues, and explicit backpressure before accepting unsustainable work.
Never discard an already committed operation to make lag look healthy. Strong reads wait or fail if the required state cannot be applied.
Corruption, bad deployment, or accidental delete
Use checksums, compatible rolling upgrades, independent versioned backups, and restore procedures.
Replication can copy corruption or a mistaken delete everywhere. It is not a substitute for backups.

Suppose A and B durably contain committed entry 42; C is only at 40. A fails. B and C still form a majority, but the election protocol must not let an out-of-date candidate discard entry 42. Raft's voting/log rules protect the committed prefix; merely selecting a reachable machine does not.
Use a tested membership/election implementation. Replication to two machines without an order/commit/election protocol is not the same guarantee.
Failure detection is suspicion, not proof

A missed heartbeat may indicate a pause or network problem, not permanent death. Per-shard elections handle authority. The management layer can delay expensive replacement/rebalancing until a separate failure threshold, balancing repair exposure against churn. Do not reduce the write quorum to “whoever is reachable” during an outage.

request/error latency by operation, leader churn, replica/log/apply lag, under-replicated shards, remaining disk, recovery bandwidth, placement skew, stale-map retries, and backup age. Use rolling maintenance that preserves each shard's required voting quorum.
Move a shard without creating two writers
“Update the consistent hash ring” is not a data migration protocol. The old bytes, live mutations, retry state, and ownership must all move coherently.

props.aria-label: Replica movement progresses from learner bootstrap through snapshot, catch-up, membership change, and old-replica retirement

children.value: enough disk, suitable load, and a valid failure domain. Record a resumable migration task and generation.
copy a consistent snapshot at included index
. It does not vote or count toward durability yet.
while normal writes continue. Match engine state, wrapper retry state, and applied position.
Change membership through the group protocol:
use the implementation's safe reconfiguration mechanism, such as joint consensus or its supported equivalent. Do not independently overwrite replica lists on each node.
publish the authoritative configuration/leader information. Old cached routes redirect; retired copies are not independent write authorities.
only after the new configuration is durable and required replicas are ready. Keep cleanup and rollback boundaries explicit.

The coordinator can crash between steps. On restart it reads the durable task/configuration state and resumes idempotently; it does not assume the last RPC either certainly failed or certainly succeeded.
Splitting a hot or oversized logical shard is different
Moving a whole range changes physical placement; splitting changes the range directory. A correct simple protocol is:
Create child ranges, with new replica groups and supported internal export/iteration to partition the parent's snapshot.
Copy a consistent parent snapshot and stream subsequent committed mutations to the appropriate child by key hash, including deletes and retry state.
Once children are nearly caught up, establish a short write barrier and a committed parent cutover position
Ensure child quorums contain the filtered parent history through
. Activate child ownership and publish the new directory generation through a durable, recoverable control-plane workflow.
Stale parent routes forward/redirect after cutover; they never independently apply new writes to the old engine. Release bounded queued/retried requests to the children.

A brief, bounded per-shard write pause is easier to reason about than unrestricted dual writes. It must fit the service's error/latency budget; do not promise literally zero interruption. If the engine cannot export/filter existing keys, move whole pre-created shards instead and acknowledge that arbitrary online splits require an additional operational capability.
Do not resurrect a deleted value

A snapshot at index 50 contains key K. A delete at 55 removes it. If a destination copies the snapshot but is activated before replaying through 55, K reappears. Copy completion is not cutover readiness; the required mutation frontier and ownership fence are the essential checks.

at an illustrative 100MB/s copy budget, versus 27.78 hours for a full 10TB image. Smaller independent units permit parallel recovery and finer placement, but more groups increase metadata, heartbeat, file, and process overhead. Neither “one huge shard” nor “one shard per key” is a free solution.
What changes if get must be strongly consistent?

: an operation appears to take effect at a point between invocation and response. A get begun after a completed put must not return a value older than that put, absent a later ordered mutation. Concurrent operations may be ordered either way consistently.
Route a strong read to the current shard leader, or obtain a leader-authorized read position for a follower.
Use the consensus implementation's safe read protocol, such as a quorum-confirmed read-index mechanism, to establish current authority and a committed read position.
Wait until the serving engine has applied through that position, then perform the local get.
If authority or the applied position cannot be established before the deadline, fail the strong read rather than silently downgrade it.

Reading from a machine labeled “leader” is insufficient: an isolated old leader may not know a new leader exists. Lease-based fast paths require their timing/clock assumptions to hold; do not invent a safe lease from an ordinary heartbeat timeout.

necessarily fetch the value from a majority of engines. A valid leader/read-index protocol can establish authority with quorum communication and read one sufficiently applied engine. The exact mechanism matters more than counting payload responses.
Why R + W > N does not, by itself, prove linearizability

Quorum intersection is useful: for a fixed replica set it ensures a read set intersects a completed write's acknowledgment set. It does not define ordering, commitment, partial-write handling, version selection, read write-back, or reconfiguration safety.
Counterexample to the naive “read two replicas and return the largest version” shortcut.
A, B, and C hold value 0. Use N=3, W=2, R=2.
A tentative write of 1 reaches only A, then times out.
The write did not reach W; its outcome is not a safe completed commit.
A read of A+B returns 1 just because it has the highest observed version.
The read exposes the partial write without making the observation stable.
A later read of B+C returns 0, with no intervening write.
The value goes backward. The simple quorum recipe is not a linearizable register.

Proper leaderless atomic-register protocols add more than the inequality, for example carefully ordered versioning and read write-back. In our chosen design, consensus defines commitment, replicas apply only committed entries, and the strong-read barrier prevents this shortcut.

A Dynamo-style design can accept writes at different coordinators and later reconcile versions. Discuss causal/version metadata, hinted handoff, anti-entropy, read repair, and a conflict policy. A last-write-wins timestamp policy is simple but may discard a concurrent update and depends on how timestamps are generated; it is not linearizable single-key overwrite semantics merely because clocks are synchronized.

Sloppy quorums may acknowledge on fallback nodes outside the usual replica set, so the simple intersection argument needs extra care. Returning siblings or requiring application merge logic also affects the “simple value” API. That trade-off may be appropriate, but it must be explicit.
A precise answer beats an overclaim

“The base design has durable ordered writes and eventual follower reads. For linearizable gets I add a current-authority read barrier and wait for application through it. During a partition, I preserve those guarantees by rejecting operations that cannot establish the required quorum, not by calling stale data strong.”
A hot shard and a hot key are different problems
Add nodes and move virtual shards according to byte occupancy and headroom.
Node addition is not instant capacity: copying and catch-up consume network, disk, and survivor resources.
A range is hot because many keys are active
Split/move ranges and spread their leaders/replicas.
Requires a supported export and safe split protocol; avoid reacting to every short burst.
One key is read extremely often
Add eligible read-only/non-voting replicas or a cache with an explicit consistency policy; coalesce duplicate reads.
More hash ranges do not divide a single key. Extra copies incur update fan-out and stale-read/invalidations concerns.
One key is written extremely often
Batch transport/log commits where semantics permit; provision the owner and rate-limit overload.
A strictly ordered single-key register still has a serialization point. Application-level key decomposition changes semantics and requires agreement.
Add shard groups, distribute leaders, batch log work, and tune apply concurrency across shards.
Replica writes, log bytes, engine writes, and compaction/repair all contribute; replication does not multiply independent write ownership.
Stream through proxies, bound in-flight bytes, pool connections, and size NICs and replication bandwidth.
QPS alone hides payload cost. Avoid fully buffering every concurrent 1MB response multiple times.
Cache maps, distribute per-shard leadership, multiplex replication work, and tune shard granularity.
One central lookup per request or an unbounded number of tiny groups creates a new bottleneck.
Throttle and parallelize selectively, prioritize under-replicated data, and reserve foreground capacity.
Fast recovery improves durability exposure but can cause a live-service brownout if it saturates survivors.
Eventual GET = proxy/routing + network + local engine read + payload transfer
PUT/DELETE acknowledgment = routing + leader queue + durable quorum commit
Visibility on a follower = commit + replication/apply lag
Strong GET = routing + authority/read barrier + wait for apply + local read
Tail under failure = detection/election or redirect + bounded retry + normal path

The engine's P99=1ms is not the distributed service's P90. Network, queuing, values, retries, and coordination dominate some workloads. A regional deployment across zones is a plausible starting point for the supplied latency ranges; inter-region synchronous replication needs a separate distance/latency budget.

Place replicas and spare capacity to support surviving traffic after failures, not only balanced healthy traffic. Measure availability by operation and overload mode. An endlessly growing queue can make a service technically reachable but functionally unavailable.
The final architecture, after each component has a purpose

We have replaced one engine endpoint with a compatible routing layer; replaced physical-node hashing with logical shards and metadata; replaced single copies with per-shard replicated logs and engines; and added recovery/movement procedures that preserve ownership and committed history.

point to the API and routing calculation first, then trace a write and each read mode. The log records, shard-map fields, acknowledgment boundary, and movement workflow are on the diagram so you can explain the mechanisms without switching to another page.
The engine remains the supplied component. Raft and etcd labels identify example coordination implementations, not a replacement KV engine.
Distributed key-value store: annotated interview whiteboard

Applications call put, get, and delete through routing proxies that cache a shard map from a metadata quorum. Writes go to the selected shard leader and an ordered replicated log; the client acknowledgment occurs after majority commitment, before every engine necessarily applies the write. Eventual reads can use eligible followers; strong reads establish current authority and an applied read barrier. Each replica wraps an unchanged local KV engine. The diagram also shows metadata and log schemas, replica state, snapshot-and-catch-up movement, and independent backups.

The public API, placement metadata, replicated-log record, local-engine boundary, and repair protocol are all visible in one picture. Read modes are deliberate: the illustrated quorum write does not automatically make every GET linearizable.
Distributed key-value service built around existing local engines

Applications use stateless routing proxies with cached shard maps. A separate replicated metadata service manages placement and configuration. Each logical shard has a leader and two replicas across zones. The wrappers replicate a durable ordered log and apply committed operations to unchanged local engines. Eventual reads can use followers, while strong reads require an authority and apply barrier. Snapshots, backups, and repair support recovery. Many independent shard groups share the physical fleet.
Stable request IDs for mutation retries
Cached map, auth, deadlines, bounded retries

The engine internals do not change. The wrapper owns distributed authority and ordered application. The management layer owns placement workflows; routing reads its cached output rather than sending every request through the manager.

What you can say while you draw
Use these as short transitions. Pause for questions; do not turn the interview into a memorized lecture.

“The local engine is given, so I will not redesign its indexes or file format. I will build routing, shard ownership, replication, and recovery around it. I will confirm the local durability and snapshot/change-stream capabilities because those determine how safely we can bootstrap existing data.”

“At one million requests per second and a rounded 90/10 split, three copies imply roughly 1.2 million local read/write operations per second before overhead. That suggests a 120-node QPS floor, but a petabyte replicated three ways already needs 300 fully used 10TB machines, or about 429 at 70% occupancy. Payload size and retained overwrite logs may raise that substantially.”

“I will put a router in front of the existing engines. A key maps to a logical hash range, and cached metadata maps that range to an owner. All three operations follow the same ownership function. This works across machines, but one copy per shard is still a durability and availability gap.”

“I prefer many virtual ranges over modulo by machine count, because I want to move selected units instead of rehashing the whole dataset. The map is separate from the request routers. A ring balances ownership statistically; a placement manager still has to enforce failure-domain separation and handle byte or QPS skew.”

“Asynchronous read replicas improve read scale, but acknowledging only the active's local write can lose acknowledged data on failover. I would instead commit mutations to a per-shard replicated log before acknowledging them. Existing engines apply that committed sequence. I would use an established consensus implementation rather than invent its election rules.”

“If the leader commits and its response is lost, a retry must not execute an old put again after a newer write. Stable request IDs and recoverable retry state matter. If a leader dies, its replacement must retain committed history, not merely be the first machine answering a health check. A minority partition cannot acknowledge new writes in this design.”

“For a replica move I add a learner, copy a consistent snapshot, replay the suffix, and use the group's safe membership-change protocol before retiring the old copy. A range split needs a stronger cutover workflow: children caught up through a parent barrier and the old writer fenced. Updating the map alone is not migration.”

“Default reads can use followers and be stale. For a linearizable get, I need current authority and an applied read barrier. Reading any machine labeled leader, or saying R plus W exceeds N, is not enough on its own. The ordering, partial-write, and failover protocol must make the guarantee real.”

“The design preserves the local engine and scales by adding shard groups and routing capacity. It protects quorum-committed data against the chosen single-zone failure and scales reads through replicas. The trade-offs are replica/log cost, eventual default reads, majority-dependent writes, and the operational complexity of safe movement. I would size recovery and failure-time traffic, not just healthy average QPS.”
Be ready to adapt without abandoning the reasoning
Can the durable-queue design satisfy the problem instead?

Yes. A partitioned, replicated, durable log can accept mutations, with storage replicas materializing them independently and reads going to applied copies. Explain the acknowledgment boundary, ordering per key/shard, each replica's complete input stream, replay offsets, deduplication, and lag. A generic work queue does not automatically broadcast each update to all replicas. At large-value write peaks, retention cost is a major design constraint.

A single active can serialize healthy-path operations, but that does not prove safe behavior after failure. An asynchronous standby may lack acknowledged writes; an old active may still believe it is authoritative. Strong semantics require a safe acknowledgment, promotion, fencing, and read protocol. State the conditions instead of repeating the shorthand.
Are client-side routers fundamentally unable to provide consistent writes?

No. Smart clients complicate version rollout, retry correctness, and stale topology handling, but consistency must be enforced at the storage/replication boundary regardless of routing placement. A buggy or old client must not turn a retired node into a legitimate writer. A proxy is an operational simplification, not the source of the write order.

In the chosen ordered-log design, a delete is retained as an ordered mutation until a consistent snapshot safely represents its effect; a restored replica must install that state and replay the proper suffix. In state-based/leaderless anti-entropy, absence alone cannot distinguish deletion from “not copied yet,” so versioned tombstones are usually necessary. Garbage-collect them only after the repair/replica-lifetime assumptions make old-value resurrection impossible, or require old replicas to be rebuilt.
What if a single key exceeds one machine's write capacity?

Moving or splitting hash ranges cannot distribute one key's strictly ordered overwrites across independent writers without changing semantics. Optimize batching/transport, provision its owner, and apply backpressure. Application-level decomposition or commutative operations might help, but they change the interface/semantics and need agreement. Extra read replicas solve a different problem.
Can we keep the same design for a 1GB value?

Not by passing 1GB to an engine capped at 1MB. Extend the wrapper's representation: store immutable, bounded-size chunks or use a blob store, and publish a versioned manifest/pointer through a single-key mutation only after all chunks are durable. Readers fetch one committed manifest and its matching chunks; deletes remove/tombstone the manifest, with delayed garbage collection for orphaned or old chunks. This adds network latency, consistency and cleanup concerns; it is an explicit follow-up, not a hidden property of the base design.
What if scans or bulk operations become required?

Hash sharding makes ordered scans scatter across shards. Add bounded fan-out, pagination/resume tokens, and clear snapshot consistency semantics, or reconsider range partitioning. Atomic multi-key/bulk operations are a larger change: independently ordered shards do not supply a global transaction or global consistent snapshot automatically.
How would you support a regional disaster?

Zone separation is not region separation. Asynchronous cross-region copies/backups provide a nonzero recovery point and a restore/promotion workflow. Synchronous cross-region consensus can reduce acknowledged-data loss under the specified failure model, but raises latency and affects quorum availability. Define recovery point, recovery time, fencing, and the failure domains before choosing.
Would erasure coding be a better durability scheme?

It can reduce storage overhead compared with three full copies, especially for large immutable/cold data or backups. It adds fragment placement, reconstruction work, degraded-read latency, and often update amplification. For a frequently overwritten low-latency KV service, full replication is a simpler base answer; evaluate erasure coding against the actual value sizes and update patterns rather than treating it as universally superior.
Why not retain the log forever and skip snapshots?

Overwrite traffic makes the log grow even when the current dataset is nearly constant, and replay time grows with historical writes rather than live data size. A 1PB current dataset can generate far more than a petabyte of logs. Consistent checkpoints, safe truncation, and resnapshotting laggards bound storage and recovery time.
How does a write receipt work after a shard split?

A receipt must identify its group/configuration context, not only a naked numeric index. The split workflow records the parent's cutover frontier included in each child, allowing a barrier to be translated or resolved by a current authority. If the implementation cannot translate a token, refresh and use a supported strong-read path rather than compare unrelated child and parent indices.
Can we keep serving during a management-plane outage?

Existing, reachable replica groups can continue under their committed membership, using cached maps and per-group leader discovery. New placement and unknown routes may fail. This is why management and request routing are separate, but it is not a promise that every operation works indefinitely with stale metadata and unreachable peers.
How do you know the 10K QPS and 1ms local latency apply?

Ask about benchmark conditions. A machine's capacity depends on payload size, read/write mix, durability mode, working-set size, network, and background repair/compaction. Use the given number for an explicit first estimate, then explain which assumptions need workload validation. Do not invent a more precise per-product benchmark in an interview.

Keep the engine. Name the owner. Route without a central bottleneck. Commit before promising durability. Apply in order. Move only with a cutover protocol. Match reads to the consistency contract. Budget failures, not just the happy path.
